newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian markets down ahead of U.S. jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Asian markets down ahead of U.S. jobs data.

text.p: Nervousness ahead of crucial U.S. jobs data and an overnight drop on Wall Street sent Asian stock markets into negative territory on Friday, with Tokyo's bourse losing more than one percent.
Hong Kong's key Hang Seng index was down marginally as investors stayed on the sidelines, but Sydney stocks lost almost one percent.
Bangkok's SET index continued its slide, finishing 1.48 percent down to a 35-month low after its seventh consecutive day of losses.
Jakarta defied the trend, edging 0.13 percent higher on speculative buying in second-liners.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average closed down 227.29 points or 1.12 percent at 20,152.53.
Brokers said the Tokyo market was bracing for the United States August employment report to be released later today.
The figures are being closely watched for indications on the future direction of interest rates amid growing fears of an increasingly robust U.S. economy.
"The bottom of the Nikkei is being supported at 20,000, but I'm not sure if it will be after the U.S. employment data," said Hiroshi Morimoto, general manager at Daiwa Securities Co Ltd.

If the U.S. figures were larger than expected, this would increase the possibility of a rate hike and dampen New York stocks. This could prompt foreign investors to sell Japanese equities to take profits, Morimoto said.
Hong Kong stocks lost 0.14 percent as investors cautiously awaited the U.S. data, analysts said. The Hang Seng index fell 14.92 points to 11,025.59.

"The fact is, interest rates are rearing their ugly head again and it is making investors think twice before jumping in, especially with the data coming out tonight," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities.

Thai stocks, which tumbled early on rumours that some brokerages may be hit by client defaults on margin loans, pared losses by the close on news that a private sector rescue fund would shore up the market.
The SET index finished 15.17 points down at 1,007.51, its lowest level since its 998.71 close in October 1993.

Brokers said the index fell to an intra-day low of 988.03 but climbed back after the Thai Bankers' Association said the fund would move into the market and state-owned Krung Thai Bank confirmed it could advance funds to do so.
Manila shares closed weaker as the market continued to be hounded by uncertainty over the direction of U.S. interest rates and the tension between the U.S. and Iraq, traders said.
The composite index dropped by 21.40 points, or 0.67 percent, to 3,170.16 points.
Brokers said Australian shares were bruised by Thursday's nervous Dow ahead of the U.S. payroll data, although selective bargain hunting helped restrict the market's fall.
The key share barometer, the All Ordinaries index, closed 20.4 points lower at 2,237.0.
Jakarta shares were higher by the close following active local speculative buying in selected second-liners. The composite index rose 0.72 points to 543.75.
"The local speculators certainly ran the show, but they failed to have much impact on the market as most of the heavyweights remained inactive," one broker said.
In late Tokyo trade, the dollar was at 109.20/25 yen and 1.4852/59 marks against its New York close of 109.17/22 yen and 1.4860/70 marks.

In Singapore, SIMEX Brent futures were higher. October settled at $22.25 a barrel, up nine cents from its last close on London's IPE. But the market remained cautious over the situation in Iraq, traders said.
Hong Kong gold closed slightly lower. Bullion ended at US$385.40/385.90 an ounce against New York's US$385.50/386.00 close on Thursday.
